title: The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky

teacherSummary.text: Marshal Jack Potter rides a Pullman car home to Yellow Sky with his new bride, anxious because he married without telling the town. Meanwhile drunken Scratchy Wilson terrorizes the empty street with revolvers, looking for his old enemy Potter. Scratchy confronts the unarmed marshal, hears he is married, says 'I s'pose it's all off now,' and walks away.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “A newly married pair had boarded this coach at San Antonio” slowly and put it in my own words: A newly married couple has boarded the Pullman train at San Antonio, heading west. Next, craft. I notice the plain, almost reporter-like sentence, which treats a wedding trip as an ordinary news item. The strongest word is “married”: the marriage is the quiet event that will end the town's gunfight days, so the plain word carries the plot. Then, effect. What does Crane want us to notice about this couple from the start? My answer: Crane opens with something tame and modern, a couple on a fancy train, to show that the tame, settled world from back east is arriving in the West; the old gunfighter will be beaten not by a bullet but by a wife.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Sensitive content: Gunplay; drunkenness. Preview the story, tell students in advance, and allow a pass on reading aloud. Keep discussion on how the writer uses these elements, not on graphic detail. This section mentions drinking or a drug (“…ed in the open door. He cried: "Scratchy Wilson's drunk, and has turned loose with both hands."…”). Treat it as period custom or plot detail; name it plainly and don't glamorize it.
contentNotes.studentPreview: Heads-up: this story includes gunplay; drunkenness.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “Why does the writer include this, and what does it make us notice?”
